newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SABENA PLAYS DOWN FURTHER IMPACT OF DEREGULATION.
newsitem.headline: SABENA PLAYS DOWN FURTHER IMPACT OF DEREGULATION.

text.p: Belgian airline Sabena SA said on Wednesday that air transport deregulation in the European Union was de facto completed as many airlines would stay out of the rat race for high-density routes.

"The deregulation which goes into effect on April 1 is just the end of (a process of) liberalisation which has already taken place," Sabena chief executive officer Paul Reutlinger told a news conference on the carrier's 1996 earnings.
He said the current situation would not change considerably, with only intra-EU flights to be liberalised.
"Sabena does not have any intention of profiting from this new possibility and I think that not many airlines are going into that business," Reutlinger said.

"Normally domestic routes with a high density of passengers already have a high density of timetables and it's very difficult to penetrate these markets unless you have very, very low costs," he said.
He noted that Sabena, which recorded a higher-than-expected 8.87 billion Belgian franc consolidated net loss in 1996, had not even completed its cost-cutting drive.
"It would be foolish for us to try and go into one of the high-density markets, such as the Frankfurt to Berlin route, or Milan to Rome," he said.
But Reutlinger said that despite deregulation, air transport was still being regulated in other ways, for instance by the lack of airport slots.
"Even if you have traffic rights to fly to certain airports, if you are not getting the slots you cannot do it," he said.
He predicted the battle for slots would be heavy and become one of the key issues in air transport.
